Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 18: Compiler Optimizations
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. Optimization preserves observations, not source layout
Problem and first experiment

SAY
An optimizer is allowed to change the route to an answer when the program's required observations stay the same. This is the as-if rule. A loop over known constants may become one constant result, and a source variable may need no storage at all. That can surprise a reader expecting one assembly instruction per statement, but it does not imply missing work. The essential question is whether every permitted input still gets the required behavior. Undefined behavior undermines that argument rather than forcing the compiler to preserve a familiar accident. We will compare valid calculations and deliberately wrong rewrites without executing invalid memory or arithmetic operations.

DO
Ask what output would establish equivalence for one test but not all inputs.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.024

------------------------------------------------------------

2. Unroll a loop and keep the remainder path
Problem and first experiment

SAY
Both functions sum the five unsigned values two, four, six, eight, and ten. The scalar loop adds them one at a time. The pair loop handles two values per iteration, then uses a remainder path for the last value ten. That is why both outputs are thirty. If we omit the remainder path, the optimized-looking version would return twenty and silently drop valid input. All values and sizes here are fixed and small, so arithmetic remains valid. We are comparing semantics, not timing: this output does not prove the pair version is faster or that a compiler emits exactly two additions per loop.

DO
Predict the pair subtotals and the final remainder contribution.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.012

------------------------------------------------------------

3. Changing copy order changes overlapping data
Problem and first experiment

SAY
Each array begins with one, two, three, four, and five. We want to move the first four values one position to the right. The forward loop writes one into position one, then reads that replaced value on its next iteration, eventually producing five ones. The backward loop reads each original value before overwriting the preceding source region and produces one, one, two, three, four. Every array access is in bounds, so this is a defined demonstration of wrong semantics rather than a memory violation. It shows why an optimization cannot freely reorder accesses when source and destination overlap.

DO
Track array contents after the first two forward iterations.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.020

------------------------------------------------------------

4. Inlining exposes context; the keyword does not command it
Problem and first experiment

SAY
If a small helper receives a known constant, bringing its operations into the caller can reveal that one branch is never needed. Inlining therefore offers more than saving a call instruction: it can enable constant folding and other simplifications across the former boundary. However, copying a large body into many callers can increase code size and strain instruction storage. The C++ inline keyword does not force machine-code substitution; it also has important definition and linkage rules. Prefer a clear helper interface, inspect compiler decisions when relevant, and measure the real workload before forcing a source rewrite that duplicates logic across callers.

DO
Use a helper with a constant Boolean argument to identify a removable branch.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.004

6. Where the simple approach fails
The chapter problem

SAY
A hand optimization that caches b before every write through a is wrong unless the design proves the storage cannot overlap.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Cache b before assigning a and assume distinct parameter names mean distinct objects.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Preserve the order or supply and enforce a stronger non-overlap contract. Test both aliasing and non-aliasing arguments.

7. Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
The chapter problem

SAY
A const reference prevents mutation through that reference; it does not prove the underlying object cannot change through another name. The write through a can therefore affect the later read through b. Optimization must preserve this allowed input case unless an additional valid non-aliasing contract excludes it.

A plausible alternative: Prefer clear code and measured compiler output before adding manual caches.

8. Chapter 18 — Compiler Optimizations
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Optimization changes an implementation while preserving the behavior required by the language and selected compilation model. It is not a promise to preserve every intermediate variable or source-level step. The strongest optimizations often come from proving that work is unnecessary, not from choosing a faster instruction for the same work.

10. Inlining
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Inlining replaces a call boundary with the callee’s operations in the caller’s optimization context. It can remove call overhead and expose constants, dead branches, and redundant work. The inline keyword in C++ has important language linkage and definition rules; it is not a command forcing machine-code substitution. Inlining can increase code size and instruction-cache pressure. A small frequently used helper may benefit, while duplicating a large cold path may hurt. Let measurement and compiler diagnostics guide the decision. The best result can be a mixture of inlined hot paths and shared out-of-line slow paths.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

11. Constant folding
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Constant folding evaluates expressions whose values are known during translation. A fixed arithmetic expression can become a literal, and a condition based on a known constant can select one path before runtime. The expression must still be meaningful under the language’s rules. A compiler is not required to preserve a runtime-looking overflow merely because the programmer wrote it as a sequence of constants. Use appropriately typed constants and checked compile-time expressions when limits matter. Compile-time calculation reduces runtime work but does not remove semantic obligations.

DO

Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.006, SP18.007

------------------------------------------------------------

12. Dead-code elimination
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Dead-code elimination removes operations whose results cannot affect required observable behavior. An unused local calculation may disappear completely. A benchmark that computes a value and never uses it can therefore measure almost no intended work. Make benchmark results observable through a legitimate output or comparison outside the timed region. Do not indiscriminately mark all data volatile; that changes the workload and can block useful optimization. The goal is to preserve the operation being measured without introducing a different memory-access contract.

DO

Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.008, SP18.009

13. Common-subexpression elimination
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
When the compiler can prove that an expression has the same value at several points, it may compute it once and reuse the result. The proof depends on whether intervening operations can change its inputs, including memory reachable through aliases. Two identical-looking loads are not necessarily redundant if another operation can modify the location. Conversely, two differently written expressions may be equivalent after simplification. Help the compiler with clear ownership, const-correct interfaces, and limited aliasing rather than duplicating manual caches whose validity is difficult to maintain.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

14. Loop unrolling
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Unrolling repeats the loop body several times per control iteration. It can reduce branch overhead and expose independent work, but it increases code size and requires a remainder path when the element count is not a multiple of the unroll factor. A correct unrolled loop handles zero elements and the final partial group without reading past the range. Performance can worsen if extra code strains instruction storage or register allocation. Unrolling is a transformation to evaluate, not a universal improvement. Vectorization and memory bandwidth may dominate the outcome.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

15. Tail-call optimization
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A call in tail position can sometimes reuse the current function’s frame rather than creating another active frame. This can turn some recursion into constant-stack iteration. Language cleanup requirements, ABI constraints, and compiler choices determine whether the transformation is possible. A local object requiring destruction after the call can prevent a simple tail transfer. Debugging options or calling-convention differences can also matter. Do not use a recursive algorithm with unbounded depth on the assumption that a compiler will always optimize it into a loop. Establish the resource bound independently.

In plain English: First make the program correct, then measure where time is really being spent before trying to make it faster.

DO

16. Strength reduction
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Strength reduction replaces an operation with an equivalent cheaper sequence in the relevant context. Multiplication by a constant might become shifts and adds, or a loop might update a pointer incrementally instead of recomputing an index product. The “cheaper” operation depends on the target. Modern processors can multiply efficiently, while a longer shift-add sequence may create more dependencies. Signed division transformations also need correct rounding for negative values. Prefer clear source and inspect generated code before manually encoding a transformation whose benefit may have disappeared on the target machine.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

17. Arithmetic transformations
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Integer and floating-point transformations obey different algebraic freedoms. Unsigned arithmetic has modular identities. Signed arithmetic can be transformed under the assumption that defined executions do not overflow. Floating-point addition is generally not associative because rounding depends on evaluation order. Options that permit reassociation or disregard special values change the numerical contract. A faster result under such options is not automatically an equivalent result for every input. Document any relaxed arithmetic assumptions, including finite-only inputs, acceptable error, and reproducibility requirements. [ R2 ]

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.

18. Aliasing restrictions
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Aliasing limits which memory operations can move past one another or reuse loaded values. C’s restrict qualifier is a promise about access relationships during a particular execution region, not a runtime check. Standard C++20 does not have a directly identical core-language restrict keyword, though compilers provide extensions. An incorrect non-aliasing promise can make an otherwise plausible loop undefined or miscompiled relative to the programmer’s intent. Use it only when the API actually excludes overlapping access patterns. The performance opportunity comes from a true invariant; annotations cannot manufacture that invariant.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

19. Optimization barriers
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A barrier limits particular transformations. Volatile access, compiler-specific assembly constraints, atomic operations, and external calls can impose different restrictions, but they are not interchangeable. A compiler barrier need not be a hardware memory fence, and a hardware fence needs a correct language-level interface. volatile is not a thread-synchronization mechanism. It serves specific observable-access roles, including some device interfaces under implementation rules. For concurrent application state, use atomics and synchronization primitives. For benchmarking, use a narrowly justified technique rather than disabling the optimizer across the entire workload.

In plain English: First make the program correct, then measure where time is really being spent before trying to make it faster.

DO

Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

20. The as-if rule
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The as-if principle allows any implementation that preserves the program’s required observable behavior. A variable can disappear, operations can combine, and a loop can become a constant when the result is known. The preserved behavior is defined by the language and relevant options, not by the programmer’s expectation of a one-to-one translation. Undefined behavior undermines the premise on which source-level reasoning depends. Optimization is therefore a reason to be more precise about validity, not a reason to avoid optimization. A well-defined program should remain correct across optimization levels even when its instructions and timing change substantially.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.

21. Optimizing a known-length calculation
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The requirement is to compute sum(3*x[i] + 1) for a bounded unsigned sequence. The source makes the arithmetic domain explicit and returns the result so it remains observable. Companion listing: ch18/transform.cpp At low optimization, the output may show an explicit loop, repeated address calculations, and a function call. At higher optimization, the compiler may inline the function, unroll or vectorize the loop, or compute the final constant because all inputs are known. Each implementation can be correct because the required result is 64. For a meaningful runtime benchmark, use runtime-supplied data with controlled size and make the final result observable outside the timed loop. Do not conclude that one optimization level has achieved an extraordinary per-element speed if the compiler has removed the per-element work entirely.

22. Constant folding and dead code
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
For int x = 4 × 8; if (0) use(x); , an optimizing compiler can replace the multiplication with constant 32 and remove the unreachable branch entirely. These transformations are legal because no permitted observation changes. Debug builds may retain more structure, so source-to-assembly correspondence depends strongly on optimization settings.

23. Aliasing blocks a load elimination
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Consider *p = 5; x = *q; . If p and q may alias, the store through p can affect the load through q . The compiler cannot generally replace the load with a previously known value of *q . Proving non-aliasing creates optimization freedom, but the proof must follow language and ABI rules.

27. An unused benchmark result can erase the benchmark
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A benchmark repeatedly calculates a sum but never uses the answer. An optimizer may remove the entire calculation because it cannot affect required behavior. The resulting short time does not mean the processor performed billions of additions for free. Make the result matter through a legitimate check or output outside the timed region, and use runtime-controlled data when measuring per-element work. Marking every variable volatile is not a neutral repair; it changes access obligations and can prevent useful transformations that production code would use. The experiment should preserve the intended work while adding as little unrelated measurement behavior as practical.

DO
Ask learners what a compiler may remove from a loop with an unused result.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.008

------------------------------------------------------------

28. Aliasing is a relationship, not a spelling difference
Reason about the implementation

SAY
The expressions through p and q may look different while naming the same storage. If code writes through p, a later load through q may observe the new value. Reusing an older cached q value would then change behavior. Our overlapping-array example expands that idea over several elements: access order becomes part of correctness. C restrict can express a particular access promise, but standard C++20 has no directly identical core-language keyword. Compiler extensions do not manufacture a true invariant. Only add such a promise when the public contract excludes the overlapping cases and callers actually satisfy that restriction.

DO
Compare independent arrays with two ranges inside one array.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.010

------------------------------------------------------------

29. Arithmetic equivalence depends on the numeric domain
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Algebra from exact arithmetic does not automatically transfer to every machine type. Floating-point addition rounds intermediate results, so regrouping a plus b plus c can change the final value. Signed integer transformations also rely on defined executions not overflowing, while unsigned arithmetic has a modular rule. A performance option that permits reassociation may be useful for a numerical workload, but it changes which observations are required to remain identical. Document the tolerated error, treatment of special values, and reproducibility needs before accepting it. The optimization review should identify the arithmetic domain instead of treating every plus sign as the same mathematical operation.

DO
Discuss a very large value, its negative, and one small addend.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.018

------------------------------------------------------------

30. A barrier limits a particular kind of reordering
Reason about the implementation

SAY
The word barrier can hide several distinct mechanisms. A compiler barrier constrains certain compiler transformations, while a hardware fence controls specified ordering at the processor level. Volatile access has its own observable-access role, often relevant to particular device interfaces, but it does not make an ordinary shared counter safe between threads. Correct synchronization needs a language-level contract the compiler understands, such as atomics or a mutex. Do not scatter volatile through a program to make an optimization concern disappear. State which accesses must be ordered, between which participants, and for what reason, then choose the mechanism that actually provides that guarantee.

DO
Separate a compiler-transformation concern from a thread-communication concern.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.022

Save the old read. remembered = 4. This value copy is independent of later changes.

Write a, then read b. x = 9; after = 9. Moving the read before the write changes observable behavior when the references alias.

34. Aliasing changes the result of a rewrite
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Aliasing changes the result of a rewrite. remembered is a value copy of b, so it preserves the old value 4.

Two references may name the same integer. Compare updating then reading through the second reference with remembering its old value first.

Different variable names do not imply different storage. This value copy is independent of later changes. Moving the read before the write changes observable behavior when the references alias.

remembered is a value copy of b, so it preserves the old value 4.

a refers to x. This write changes x to 9 and therefore changes what a later read through b sees.

b also refers to x, so this later read yields 9. Reusing remembered here would violate the required order when arguments alias.

a and b both name x. A value captured before a write cannot replace a later read through an alias without changing the result.

A hand optimization that caches b before every write through a is wrong unless the design proves the storage cannot overlap. In the extended lab: Cache b before assigning a and assume distinct parameter names mean distinct objects.

45. Chapter summary and maintenance
Recall and transfer

SAY
A const reference prevents mutation through that reference; it does not prove the underlying object cannot change through another name. The write through a can therefore affect the later read through b. Optimization must preserve this allowed input case unless an additional valid non-aliasing contract excludes it.

Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. Prefer clear code and measured compiler output before adding manual caches.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Cache b before assigning a and assume distinct parameter names mean distinct objects. Preserve the order or supply and enforce a stronger non-overlap contract. Test both aliasing and non-aliasing arguments.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

------------------------------------------------------------

46. Tail position does not guarantee constant stack use
Recall and transfer

SAY
A function whose last apparent action is another call may be a candidate for tail-call optimization. Yet a local object that must be destroyed after that call adds required work, and the ABI or compiler configuration may prevent the simple transformation. Do not accept arbitrary recursion depth because one optimized build happened to use a jump. The input and resource contract must be safe independently unless the environment explicitly guarantees the needed transformation. An iterative version with an explicit data structure can make the resource bound easier to state. Performance evidence from one build is useful, but it is not a portable lifetime or stack guarantee.

DO
Ask where a local destructor would run relative to the final call.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch18.json → SP18.014

------------------------------------------------------------

47. Use a correctness experiment and a performance experiment
Recall and transfer

SAY
The paired loop should first be tested on empty, one-element, odd-length, and even-length ranges. Only after those results agree with the baseline should we ask whether the change helps performance. Generate code at several optimization levels and identify transformations supported by the actual listing rather than guessing from a flag name. Then measure a controlled workload whose data and result cannot disappear. Record compiler options and machine context with the result. This separates two claims that are often mixed together: the program computes the right answer, and this implementation is faster under these measured conditions. Either claim needs its own evidence.

DO
Require a boundary-test plan before accepting a benchmark chart.
